value.overview: The Yellow-backed Oriole (Icterus chrysater) is a medium-sized New World oriole of the family Icteridae. Adults are strikingly patterned, with bright yellow underparts and back contrasting with a black face, throat, wings, and tail. The species inhabits tropical forest edges, scrub, open woodland, plantations, and other partly open landscapes. It is mainly a resident bird across its range, but its distribution is patchy in Central America, and it is an exceptionally rare accidental visitor in Costa Rica.
value.classification: The Yellow-backed Oriole belongs to the family Icteridae, which includes orioles, blackbirds, grackles, and caciques. It is classified in the genus Icterus, the New World orioles.
value.identification: Adults show a bold black-and-yellow pattern: the face, throat, wings, and tail are black, while the back and underparts are bright yellow. The bill is dark, and there are no obvious white wingbars. Females resemble males but may have slightly duller or greener yellow areas. Immature birds are generally more olive-colored and have browner flight feathers. The species can be confused with other yellow-and-black orioles, so distribution and detailed plumage marks are important.
value.rangeHabitat: The Yellow-backed Oriole occurs from southern Mexico and parts of northern Central America southward through Panama and into northern South America, including Colombia and Venezuela. Its distribution is discontinuous, with a notable gap through much of Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is considered accidental or exceptionally rare, with documented records including the Portalón de Aguirre area near Quepos in 2013 and 2014. Elsewhere, it uses forest edges, scrub, open woodland, pine-oak habitats, deciduous woodland, cloud-forest edges, plantations, and secondary growth, from low elevations to roughly 2,900 meters.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident and non-migratory. In Costa Rica it is not a regular migrant; records are accidental and extremely rare, apparently involving individuals outside the species’ normal distribution rather than a predictable seasonal movement.
value.breeding: Detailed breeding information for the Yellow-backed Oriole is limited, but it follows the general reproductive pattern of many Icterus orioles. The species is believed to build a woven, hanging nest from plant fibers, usually suspended from vegetation. Eggs of this group are pale or whitish with darker markings, often concentrated toward the broader end. Breeding is associated with the local rainy or warmer season in different parts of its range, but timing can vary geographically.
value.dietFeeding: The Yellow-backed Oriole feeds on a varied diet that includes fruit, nectar, and arthropods. It may forage in shrubs, trees, forest edges, and cultivated areas, taking insects and other small invertebrates from foliage and consuming soft fruits and floral nectar. It has been reported from banana plantations and may occasionally feed on cultivated bananas, although it is primarily a generalist fruit- and insect-eating bird.
value.behavior: This oriole usually forages actively in vegetation, moving through foliage and along woodland edges in search of fruit, nectar, and insects. Its contrasting plumage makes adults conspicuous in open habitats, while immature birds can be less obvious because of their greener tones. It may occur singly or in pairs. As a resident species over most of its range, it is not known for long-distance migration, and its behavior in Costa Rica is poorly documented because records there are so rare.

conservation.populationTrend: A precise global population trend is not well documented. The species has a broad range and is considered adaptable to modified and partly open habitats.
